description: From Egypt to China, the bird that rises from its own ashes travels through civilizations. One shared dream: that destruction is never final.

hero.hook: A bird dies in the fire and comes back. Why did so many cultures invent the same dream?

blocks.text: The **Phoenix** is the bird of fire that is reborn from its own ashes. More than a creature out of a story, it carries a human dream: **resurrection**, renewal, the triumph of life over death.
From the Nile valley to the palaces of China, the figure changes shape. The idea stays the same: what burns can start again. Here is how the myth travels, from ancient Egypt to our rebuilt cities.
The ancestor of the Phoenix is Egyptian: the **Bennu**. Its name comes from a verb meaning “to shine” or “to rise.” It was often shown as a heron, not as a bird of prey in flames.

blocks.caption: The Bennu, sacred heron linked to the sun and to creation

blocks.text: According to the priests of [[Heliopolis]], the city of sun worship, the Bennu was the first living being on the **Benben Stone**, the hill that rose out of the liquid chaos. Its cry opened time. Linked to the sun god **Ra**, then to **Osiris**, god of the dead, it promised the cycle: the sun dies every evening and is reborn every morning.
The gray heron, the likely model for the Bennu, often stands still facing the rising sun. The Egyptians saw in that pose an act of solar worship.

The Greek historian **Herodotus** turned the Bennu into the **Phoenix**: a rare bird with red and gold feathers that returns every **500 years**. The Romans, among them the poet **Ovid** and the naturalist **Pliny the Elder**, gave it its spectacular ending.

blocks.caption: The Phoenix bursts into flame: destruction and rebirth in one gesture

blocks.text: The Phoenix is unique. When it weakens, it builds a nest of spices, cinnamon, myrrh and nard. The sun, or the beating of its own wings, sets it alight. A young bird is born from the ashes. It carries the remains of its elder to the altar of the sun in Egypt.
For Rome the bird became a symbol of **Aeternitas**, the eternity of the Empire. Later, Christians would read in it the image of the resurrection.

sections.title: The Greeks and Romans invent the pyre

blocks.text: In China, the [[Chinese Fenghuang]] is not really a bird that burns. It is a creature of harmony, often tied to the **empress**. Its appearance announces a just ruler or an era of peace.

blocks.caption: The Fenghuang: omen of peace and imperial symbol

blocks.text: In Japan the **Hōō** plays a similar part. You can see it on temple roofs in [[Kyoto]] and on **10,000 yen** notes. Here the bird speaks less about survival after death than about moral and cosmic balance.

sections.title: In Asia, another bird of virtue

blocks.text: In the Middle Ages, alchemists turned the Phoenix into a metaphor. The [[transmutation]] of metals, and above all the dark phase called [[nigredo]], recalls its cycle: you have to destroy in order to purify. [[The Phoenix in medieval alchemy]] became an image of the spirit reborn.
The city of **Phoenix**, in Arizona, was given that name in **1867**. It rose on the canals and ruins of the Hohokam civilization, gone for centuries.
Other cousin birds live around the world: the Persian **Simurgh**, the **Anqa** of Islamic tradition. Everywhere the same need: to believe that destruction is not final.

From the Egyptian **Bennu** to the Greco-Roman Phoenix and the Asian **Fenghuang**, the bird of renewal ties together sun, fire and immortality. A universal myth to say that you can rise again after the fire.

sections.title: From alchemists to cities that rise again
